client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away a few weeks ago. I keep losing focus at work, like I'll be in the middle of something and suddenly my mind just goes blank, or I find myself crying at my desk for no obvious reason. I'm not sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd at least try.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for giving this a try, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that takes real courage. Losing your grandmother is a profound loss, and what you're describing — the blank moments, the unexpected tears — sounds like grief finding its way out even when you're trying to carry on. It makes complete sense that your mind and heart are struggling to stay present right now. Can you tell me a little about her, and what her loss has meant to you personally?

client: She was honestly one of the only people in my life who I felt really understood me, you know? Like I could call her about anything and she'd just listen without judging or trying to fix it. Now that she's gone, there's this quiet that I didn't expect, and it makes me realize how much I was leaning on her without even knowing it.
therapist: What you're describing — losing someone who truly *got* you — is such a deep and particular kind of loss, and it makes sense that the quiet she left behind feels so disorienting. It sounds like she wasn't just your grandmother, but also a real anchor for you, and now you're becoming aware of that weight you were carrying together. I'm curious — when you notice that quiet, or find yourself wanting to reach for the phone to call her, what kinds of thoughts tend to come up for you in those moments?

client: Honestly, the first thing that hits me is this wave of guilt, like I didn't call her enough when she was alive, or I'd cancel plans with her because I was too busy with work. And then I start thinking that she probably felt lonely or forgotten, and that's a really hard thing to sit with. It's like grief and guilt are kind of tangled up together for me, and I can't always tell where one ends and the other begins.
therapist: That tangled feeling of grief and guilt is such a painful place to sit, and I really hear how much weight you're carrying in those moments of missing her. I want to gently ask you something — when you imagine your grandmother looking back at your relationship, do you think she saw someone who didn't care enough, or is it possible she saw someone she loved deeply, even with the busyness of life getting in the way sometimes? What do you think *she* would have said about how much you meant to her?

client: I know in my head that she loved me and she probably wasn't sitting there keeping score of missed calls. But when I try to actually feel that, it doesn't really land, like I can tell myself the logical thing but it doesn't touch the guilt. I guess I'm a little skeptical of that kind of reframing because it almost feels like I'm just letting myself off the hook for something I genuinely did wrong.
therapist: What you're pointing to is actually really important — there's a difference between reframing something to escape discomfort, and genuinely working through what you're responsible for, and it sounds like you don't want to shortcut that process. Rather than trying to logic the guilt away, it might be worth asking: is there something specific you wish you'd done differently that feels unfinished or unacknowledged — not to punish yourself, but to actually honor it? What would it look like to take that guilt seriously without letting it become the whole story of who you were to her?

client: There's one specific thing that keeps coming back to me, which is that she asked me to visit for her birthday last year and I told her I was too swamped with a work deadline, and then that birthday ended up being her last one. I think that's the thing I can't get past, because it wasn't just a missed call, it was a choice I made when I could have chosen differently. I hear what you're saying about honoring it rather than punishing myself, but I'm not really sure what that distinction looks like in practice.
therapist: That moment clearly carries so much weight for you, and I want to acknowledge that — it was a real choice, and sitting with that honestly rather than brushing it aside actually speaks to how much you loved her. Honoring it rather than punishing yourself might look like this: punishment keeps you locked in a loop of "I am someone who failed her," while honoring it asks "what does this tell me about what I value, and how do I carry that forward?" I'm wondering — if you could speak to her now about that missed birthday, what would you most want her to know?

client: I think I'd want her to know that I'm sorry, and that it wasn't that I didn't want to be there, it's that I kept assuming there would be more time. That's the part that really gets me, that I just took for granted that she'd always be there for the next birthday or the next visit. I guess I can see the difference you're drawing between punishment and honoring it, but actually saying that out loud to her, even just imagining it, feels really uncomfortable, like I'm not sure I'm ready to go there yet.
therapist: What you just said — that you kept assuming there would be more time — feels like the real heart of this, and saying it out loud, even here, took something. It's okay that fully going there doesn't feel accessible yet; grief and guilt this tender don't have to be rushed, and there's no right timeline for when you'll feel ready. For now, I'm just curious — does it feel like any small part of you received what you just said, even a little?

client: Maybe a small part, yeah, like saying it out loud made it feel more real instead of just this noise in my head that I keep trying to push down. But it also made me feel kind of exposed, and I'm already wondering if I'm going to go home tonight and just feel worse because I opened something up without really resolving it. I guess that's one of my fears about therapy, that I'll leave a session feeling more raw than when I came in.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense, and I want to be honest with you — sometimes sessions do end with things feeling more open than closed, and that rawness is real. But what you're describing, that something shifted from "noise I push down" to something you could actually name and say out loud, isn't the same as leaving with a wound reopened; it's more like the beginning of it being able to breathe. What do you think might help you feel a little more grounded tonight, even just something small, so you're not carrying this completely alone when you walk out the door?

client: Honestly, my first instinct is to say I'll just watch something on TV and zone out, but I know that's really just avoiding it rather than actually grounding myself. I think part of the problem is that most of the people I'd normally reach out to in a moment like this, I don't feel close enough to them to talk about something this heavy, which is something I've been realizing more and more since she died. It's like she was kind of my one safe person, and now I'm not sure who fills that role.
therapist: What you're naming here is really significant — that losing her didn't just mean losing a person, but losing the one relationship where you felt truly safe to be yourself, and that's a particular kind of loneliness that deserves to be taken seriously. It makes sense that zoning out feels easier than sitting with that, and I don't want to dismiss that sometimes rest is okay too — but I hear that you already sense the difference between resting and hiding. I'm wondering, as we think about the longer road ahead, whether part of what you might want to explore is what made her feel so safe to you — because understanding that might help you recognize or even build that kind of connection with others over time. Does that feel like something worth looking at together?

client: Yeah, I think that does feel worth exploring, but I also have this worry that even if I figure out what made her safe, I'm not sure I have the energy or the trust to try to build that with someone new right now. Like the idea of being vulnerable with someone and having them not really get it, or say the wrong thing, almost feels worse than just staying lonely. I guess I'm not sure if I'm ready to open myself up to that kind of disappointment on top of everything else I'm already feeling.
therapist: That makes so much sense — you're already carrying a lot, and the idea of reaching out and not being met with the same care she offered feels like a risk that might just add another hurt on top of everything else. What I notice though is that you're not saying you never want that connection, just that you're not sure you have the capacity for it *right now*, and that's actually a really important and self-aware distinction. I'm wondering — do you think part of what made her safe was something that built gradually over time too, or did that sense of being understood feel present with her from early on?

client: I think it built over time, honestly, like when I was younger I didn't even fully appreciate how safe she felt, it just kind of crept up on me as I got older and realized not everyone listens the way she did. So I guess there's something almost hopeful in that, the idea that it doesn't have to be instant. But then I also think about how much time that took, and how she's been in my life since the beginning, and I wonder if I can really replicate that kind of history with someone new when I'm already in my thirties.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in the fact that you found that thread of hope yourself just now — that safety can grow slowly, without pressure — and I don't want that to get lost even as the doubt comes in behind it. You're right that you can't replicate the specific history you had with her, and I don't think that's actually what you'd be looking for; what you'd be building is something new, shaped by who you are now, and the person in their thirties who knows what real listening feels like is actually better equipped to recognize and nurture that than the younger version of you was. I'm curious — are there any people already in your life, even loosely, where you've caught even a small glimpse of that quality of being heard?
